title: Indian temple architecture: Nagara, Dravida and Vesara styles
seo_title: Indian Temple Architecture: Nagara, Dravida, Vesara Styles
meta_description: Indian temple architecture explained: Nagara, Dravida and Vesara styles, the parts of a temple, regional schools, rock-cut to structural temples and key sites.
keywords: evolution of temple architecture in india
summary: Indian temple architecture is usually grouped into three styles: Nagara in the north, with a curved tower called a shikhara; Dravida in the south, with a stepped pyramidal vimana and large gateway towers called gopurams; and Vesara, the mixed forms of the Deccan. All developed from rock-cut shrines into structural temples between about the 5th and 13th centuries CE.

sections.h2: What makes a temple a temple?
paras: A Hindu temple is first of all a house for an image. Its core is a small, dark sanctum, the garbhagriha ('womb chamber'), where the main image is placed. Everything else, the halls, porches, towers, walls and enclosures, grows around this centre and leads the visitor towards it. Jain temples follow similar principles, and Buddhist architecture developed its own forms in stupas and chaitya halls.

Temples were also institutions. They owned land, employed priests, musicians, dancers, cooks and accountants, ran schools and kitchens, and were recorded in hundreds of inscriptions. Reading a temple means reading its plan, its tower, its sculpture and its inscriptions together. Our lecture [Reading a temple](how-to-read-a-temple.html) teaches exactly this, and [Temples as social institutions](temples-as-social-institutions.html) looks at the people around them.
The vocabulary differs between north and south, but most temples share the same basic parts. Learning these terms makes any temple easier to understand.
list: Garbhagriha: the sanctum that holds the main image, usually square and without windows.

Shikhara or vimana: the tower over the sanctum. In the north the tower itself is called shikhara; in the south the whole sanctum with its tower is the vimana, and shikhara means only the crowning dome.
Mandapa: a pillared hall in front of the sanctum for worshippers, music and ritual. Large temples have several.
Antarala: the vestibule joining sanctum and hall.
Pradakshina patha: the path for walking around the sanctum, inside or outside.
Adhishthana or jagati: the moulded base or raised platform.
Amalaka and kalasha: the ribbed disc and pot that crown a Nagara tower.
Gopuram: the gateway tower in the enclosure wall of a south Indian temple.
Prakara: the enclosure wall, sometimes several concentric ones.

sections.h2: From rock-cut caves to structural temples
paras: The earliest religious architecture in India that survives in stone is rock-cut. The Barabar caves in Bihar, cut under Ashoka for the Ajivika sect in the 3rd century BCE, copy timber huts in polished granite. Buddhist chaitya halls and monasteries followed in the Western Ghats at Bhaja, Karla and Kanheri, and Jain caves at Udayagiri and Khandagiri in Odisha. Our programme on [rock-cut sacred architecture](rock-cut-sacred-architecture.html) traces this tradition.

Rock-cut work continued for centuries alongside building. Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta and Badami contain Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves. The climax is the Kailasa temple at Ellora, cut in the 8th century under the Rashtrakutas from the top of a hill downwards as a complete free-standing temple.

The first surviving structural temples date from the Gupta period, around the 5th century CE: Temple 17 at Sanchi, a flat-roofed shrine with a porch, the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh with an early tower, and the brick temple at Bhitargaon. From the 6th and 7th centuries, the Chalukyas at Aihole and Badami and the Pallavas at Mahabalipuram experimented with both northern and southern forms. Our session on [early structural temples](early-structural-temples.html) covers this phase.

sections.h2: Nagara style: temples of northern India
paras: The [Nagara style](nagara-temple-architecture.html) is defined by its curvilinear tower. In the basic form, called latina, a single curved shikhara rises over the sanctum, topped by an amalaka and kalasha. Later builders added miniature towers clustered around the main one (the shekhari form, as at Khajuraho) or built towers with horizontal tiers (the bhumija form, common in Malwa).

Nagara temples usually stand on a raised platform and lack the large enclosure walls typical of the south. Regional schools developed within the style, including Odisha's Kalinga architecture, the Solanki or Maru-Gurjara temples of Gujarat and Rajasthan, and the Chandela temples of Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh.

sections.h2: Dravida style: temples of southern India
paras: The [Dravida style](dravida-temple-architecture.html) builds the tower as a stepped pyramid of storeys, each lined with miniature shrines, crowned by a dome-like shikhara. Pallava temples at Mahabalipuram and Kanchipuram, especially the Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha, show its early development in the 7th and 8th centuries.

Under the Cholas, the vimana reached monumental scale at the Brihadishvara temple in Thanjavur, completed around 1010 CE. From about the 12th century, the emphasis shifted outward: gopurams over the gateways grew taller than the central tower, and temples became walled complexes with tanks, halls and streets, as at Madurai, Srirangam and Chidambaram. Our [South India temple architecture](south-india-temple-architecture.html) journey visits several of these.

sections.h2: Vesara and the temples of the Deccan
paras: Vesara is a term found in some medieval texts for a third, mixed style. Scholars use it loosely for temples in the Deccan, especially in Karnataka, that combine features of Nagara and Dravida. How precisely the word should be applied is debated, which is why our programme is titled [Deccan temple forms and Vesara debates](deccan-temple-forms-vesara-debates.html).

The Deccan was a meeting ground. At Aihole and Pattadakal under the Early Chalukyas, Nagara and Dravida temples stand side by side. Later Chalukyas of Kalyani and the Hoysalas developed star-shaped plans, finely turned pillars and dense sculpture, as at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura. The Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.
The table gives typical features. Many temples mix them, and regional variation within each style is large.

paras: Within and beyond the three broad styles, India has many regional schools, each with its own vocabulary of plan, tower and ornament.

Hill regions developed their own forms too: timber and stone temples in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, Kashmir's stone temples with pyramidal roofs and trefoil arches at Martand and Avantipur, and the brick and terracotta temples of Bengal, with curved bangla roofs copied from village huts, at Bishnupur.
list: Kalinga (Odisha): rekha deul tower and pidha deul hall, from the Parashurameshvara to the Lingaraja in Bhubaneswar and the Sun Temple at Konark. See [Kalinga temple architecture](kalinga-temple-architecture.html).
Chandela (Khajuraho): temples on high platforms with clustered spires and dense sculpture, built about 950 to 1050 CE. See [Khajuraho architecture deep dive](khajuraho-architecture-deep-dive.html).
Solanki or Maru-Gurjara (Gujarat and Rajasthan): richly carved temples such as the Sun Temple at Modhera and the Jain temples at Mount Abu and Ranakpur.
Chola (Tamil Nadu): monumental vimanas at Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram.
Hoysala (Karnataka): stellate plans and soapstone carving at Belur and Halebidu.
Kakatiya (Telangana): the Ramappa temple at Palampet, a UNESCO site since 2021.
Vijayanagara (Karnataka): large complexes with pillared halls and gopurams at Hampi.
Kerala: temples with sloping tiled or copper roofs, circular shrines and wooden structures adapted to heavy rain.

paras: Temple walls carry a programme of images: deities in niches facing the cardinal directions, guardians at the door, river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna on the doorframe, and friezes of animals, dancers, couples and scenes from the epics and Puranas. Identifying a figure depends on its attributes, posture and position. Our [temple sculpture and iconography](temple-sculpture-iconography.html) programme and the [Identifying sculpture](reading-sculpture.html) workshop teach these conventions.

Inscriptions on walls, pillars and plinths record who paid for the temple, gifts of land and cattle, the staff it supported and later repairs. They are the main source for the social history of temples and are covered in [Temple inscriptions and patrons](temple-inscriptions-patrons.html).

A short list for anyone planning visits: Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal (Karnataka) for early experiments; Mahabalipuram (Tamil Nadu) for Pallava rock-cut and structural work; Ellora (Maharashtra) for the Kailasa; Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh) for Chandela Nagara; Bhubaneswar and Konark (Odisha) for Kalinga; Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram for the Cholas; Belur and Halebidu for the Hoysalas; Modhera (Gujarat) for the Solanki style; and Hampi for Vijayanagara.

Several of these are UNESCO World Heritage Sites; our [list of UNESCO sites in India](unesco-world-heritage-sites-in-india.html) has the full set. A good way to see the development in one trip is our study visit to [Pattadakal and Aihole](pattadakal-and-aihole-temple-design-laboratory.html), where the Early Chalukyas tried almost every option in a few kilometres, or the [Temples of eastern India](temples-of-eastern-india.html) journey through Odisha.

Start with plan and elevation. At any temple, walk around it first, count the projections on the wall, trace the path from gateway to sanctum and look at how the tower is built up. Then look at the sculpture, then the inscriptions. A notebook and a simple measured sketch teach more than a hundred photographs. Our [temple architectural documentation lab](temple-architectural-documentation-lab.html) trains students to record temples properly.

For reading, Adam Hardy's work on Indian temple architecture, George Michell's The Hindu Temple and the Encyclopaedia of Indian Temple Architecture published by the American Institute of Indian Studies are standard. For a structured course, our [Understanding Indian temple architecture](understanding-indian-temple-architecture.html) course runs from first principles to regional styles.

faq.q: What are the three styles of Indian temple architecture?
faq.a: Nagara in northern India, with a curved tower called shikhara; Dravida in southern India, with a stepped pyramidal vimana and gateway gopurams; and Vesara, a term used for the mixed forms of the Deccan, especially Karnataka, that combine features of both.

faq.q: What is the difference between Nagara and Dravida style?
faq.a: Nagara temples have a curvilinear tower topped by an amalaka, stand on raised platforms and rarely have enclosure walls. Dravida temples have a stepped pyramidal tower topped by a dome-like shikhara, and are enclosed by walls with gateway towers called gopurams.
The garbhagriha, or womb chamber, is the small, usually windowless sanctum at the heart of a Hindu temple where the main image is placed. The tower rises directly above it.

faq.q: Which is the oldest temple in India?
faq.a: Among structural temples, Temple 17 at Sanchi, the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh and the brick temple at Bhitargaon, all from around the 5th century CE, are among the oldest surviving. Earlier shrines were built of perishable materials or cut into rock.

A gopuram is a monumental gateway tower in the enclosure wall of a south Indian temple. From about the 12th century, gopurams grew so large that at temples such as Madurai and Srirangam they dominate the skyline more than the central shrine.

faq.q: Why is Pattadakal important for temple architecture?
faq.a: Pattadakal in Karnataka has 7th and 8th century Early Chalukya temples in both Nagara and Dravida styles standing side by side. It shows architects experimenting with both traditions in one place, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

faq.q: Is temple architecture important for UPSC?
faq.a: Yes. Temple architecture is a regular part of the art and culture syllabus. Questions often cover the three styles, regional schools, rock-cut architecture, dynasties and their temples, and the meaning of terms such as shikhara, vimana, mandapa and gopuram.

posts.hook: North or south? Look at the tower.
posts.caption: A curved tower topped by a ribbed disc is Nagara. A stepped pyramid with a small dome on top is Dravida. Now look at the gateways: tall gopurams mean south.
